system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2129-02-27 17:27:00 to 2129-03-06 13:43:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted after a mechanical fall resulting in a right trimalleolar ankle fracture and bilateral leg ulcers with cellulitis. She had a history of COPD, diastolic heart failure, diabetes, and polysubstance abuse. Shortly after admission, she developed hypercarbic respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. She was treated for suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia with vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam, and a course of steroids for COPD exacerbation. Due to difficulty weaning, she underwent tracheostomy placement on hospital day 17. She also experienced acute renal failure, likely prerenal from hyperglycemia, which improved with IV fluids; lasix and lisinopril were discontinued. Multifocal atrial tachycardia was managed with metoprolol. Her leg infection resolved with antibiotics, and wound care was continued. She was weaned to a trach collar, mental status improved, and she was transferred to extended care for ongoing rehabilitation and trach management.

overnight with stable oxygenation 90-94% on 1LNC. The patient 
was continued on nebs, prednisone 40 mg, and levofloxacin given 
her productive cough. Her mental status improved by day two of 
her hospital course, and she was called out to the floor.

# Respiratory distress - likely multifactorial, but given her 
initial presentation of productive cough, somlenence and 
hypercarbia, COPD was high on the differential. After she was 
sent from the MICU, this appeared to be resolved and her main 
issue at ___ was her chronic congestive heart failure and her 
hypercarbia from obesity/hypoventilation syndrome.  We continued 
her COPD treatment with albuterol and ipratropium.  In addition, 
she got one dose of 40mg prednisone before it became clear that 
her SOB was more related to her CHF and less to her COPD, so 
this was dicsontinued.   We gave her a 5 day course of 
levofloxacin, which she finished without complication.  We gave 
her IV lasix PRN (she responded well to 40mg IV lasix), and put 
her on a 1500 cc fluid restriction and she was -6L from 
admission.  We then switched her to PO lasix 60mg QD.  Physical 
therapy saw her and reported she was okay to go home as long as 
she used her walker while there.  We attempted to wean pt's O2, 
and she was satting 95% on RA.  However, we did an ambulatory O2 
saturation on her and she was satting 81-82% on RA and 87-89% on 
2L NC O2.  She was to be sent home with home O2, but per her 
assisted living facility she smokes in her room, so this was not 
possible.  We kept her and continued to diurese another 3L off 
her with 60mg PO lasix QD and the 1500cc fluid restriction, and 
upon repeat ambulatory O2 sat she only went down to 89% on RA at 
her lowest reading.  She was therefore able to be sent home not 
on home O2.  We kept her on the 60mg PO lasix (instead of her 
preivous 40mg home dose), as she will almost certainly not 
adhere to a fluid restriction at home.  We plan to have her chem 
7 drawn in 5 days, and sent to her PCP, as well as get every 
other day weights from ___ until it is clear that the 60mg PO 
lasix is not overdiuresing her.  Her discharge weight on 
standing scale was 128.6kgs.

floroquinolones. So,

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re here because you were having trouble breathing. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I’ve been feeling more short of breath, even when I’m just sitting. And I’ve been really tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was it worse with activity at first, or did it come on suddenly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started with walking, but now I can’t even lie flat. I’ve been sleeping in a chair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called orthopnea. And any cough or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had a cough with some green mucus. But no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The team found your oxygen was low when you came in—84% on room air. It got better with oxygen, but your breathing was still labored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt kind of foggy too. Still do a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood test showed high CO2, which can make you sleepy. That’s why we’re monitoring you closely. We think this is a mix of your COPD, heart failure, and your sleep apnea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your heart is enlarged, and the chest X-ray shows fluid buildup in your lungs. Your BNP was high—1200—which points to heart strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart failure before. But I thought I was okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s flared up. You’ve also gained about 20 pounds recently—mostly fluid. We’re giving you IV Lasix to help remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. My legs have been swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have edema. We’re also treating you with antibiotics—levofloxacin—for your cough, just in case it’s a lung infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray doesn’t show pneumonia, but your symptoms suggest a COPD flare. We started steroids too, but stopped them after one dose because your breathing seems more related to heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. What about the CPAP? They tried it in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You kept removing the mask. We understand it’s uncomfortable, but it helps with your breathing, especially with obesity hypoventilation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t like it. I won’t use it at home either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep encouraging it, but we know compliance is tough. For now, we’re focusing on getting your fluid down and your breathing stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat chest X-ray shows no change—still cardiomegaly and mild congestion. But no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re stable. Your oxygen is better—94% on 2 liters. We’re keeping you on the fluid restriction—1500 cc per day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s not much. I’m thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard. But too much fluid makes your heart work harder. We’ve already removed about 6 liters—you’re down to 128.6 kg from when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wow, that’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching you from IV to oral Lasix—60 mg daily, up from 40 mg. You’ll stay on that at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the increase?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because we’re worried you won’t stick to the fluid limit at home. The higher dose helps prevent fluid from building up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another walking test today to check your oxygen levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’d I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On room air, your oxygen dipped to 81%. We were going to send you home on oxygen, but your facility said you smoke in your room.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I know I shouldn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a fire hazard with oxygen. So we’re keeping you a few more days to remove more fluid. We’ll retest your oxygen after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t go home yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. But if we get your oxygen stable without needing home oxygen, you can go home sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your repeat walking test shows your oxygen only dropped to 89% on room air. That’s safe for discharge without oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re still keeping you on 60 mg Lasix and the fluid limit until discharge. Your heart function is low-normal—nothing new there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diabetes? I didn’t get my metformin yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it while you were sick, but we’ve restarted it. You’re now on 500 mg twice a day—same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All continued. We added aspirin for heart protection and Advair for your COPD—better than Symbicort for long-term control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try to keep up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your meds, especially the new Lasix and Advair. We’ll check your blood work in 5 days. And weigh yourself every other day—let your doctor know if you gain more than 2 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back. Also, avoid smoking—especially if you ever need oxygen in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today. Your daughter will be here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You look great. Keep using your walker for safety. And your home health doctor will visit within 3 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready for him.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we’re sending you with adult diapers. You mentioned some incontinence, and we want you to be comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… thanks. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of COPD, diastolic heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, and obesity hypoventilation syndrome was admitted for acute respiratory distress with hypercarbia and hypoxia. She presented with worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, productive cough, and a 20-pound weight gain due to fluid retention. Initial management in the MICU included non-invasive ventilation, IV diuresis with Lasix, antibiotics for a COPD flare, and discontinuation of steroids once heart failure was determined to be the primary issue. Her mental status improved, and she was transitioned to oral Lasix at an increased dose of 60 mg daily due to poor expected adherence to fluid restrictions. Repeat ambulatory oxygen testing initially showed desaturation to 81% on room air, but after additional diuresis, her oxygen remained above 89%, allowing discharge without home oxygen. She was restarted on metformin, continued on psychiatric medications, and discharged with new prescriptions for aspirin and Advair. A home health visit was arranged within 72 hours.
